Yes, by design: it runs on your box, so it may use owner.command, and your node signs the command. It can't sign one itself: its own key would be refused.
What's missing is only the wire to your node's door. Today the node starts an app server without telling it where the door is (startServerJob sets no SPIRIT_CALLBACK_URL), and spirit.core.ask only works inside a page. That's step 2: hand every server process the door address, and let spirit.core.ask use it outside a page. Then grantFace calls owner.command like any page does.
Go! = build it in the order 1) api, 2) the door for server processes, 3) grantFace.

Agreed, peerPost is the wire to the face: owner.command is peerOwnerPost, signed with your node's key. What I called 'the wire' was the short hop before that: grantFace, a separate process on your box, asking your node to send the command. grantFace can't send it through peerPost itself, because it has its own key (appServer.js:614) and the face obeys only yours. So it has to ask your node to sign, and that ask is a loopback call to your node's door, which a server process can't make today. If you mean grantFace should run with your node's own key instead, so it IS the owner on the wire, say so. That's a different, simpler shape.

My misread, sorry. So: a member calls 'api' on the owner's node over peerPost, like any packet. That's the wire for introspection and for calls like { grantFace: { grant: {...} } }, and it has nothing to do with the face. Recorded that way.
The grantFace-to-face path is separate, and you've already ruled it: grantFace runs on your box and uses owner.command, which your node signs. Nothing else on it needs your answer. The build order is still 1) api over peerPost, 2) the door for server processes, 3) grantFace, waiting on your Go!.
